content: A molecule released during exercise could help muscles fight the weakness and fatigue that make staying active so difficult for many people with type 2 diabetes. Exercise does more than burn calories and build strength. It triggers a complex series of chemical signals that help muscles become stronger, more efficient, and more resistant to fatigue. But for people with type 2 diabetes, muscle weakness and declining endurance can make it difficult to stay active, creating a cycle that may worsen their condition. Researchers at the University of Leeds have identified a molecule that could help break that cycle. Known as L-β-aminoisobutyric acid (L-BAIBA), this naturally occurring compound acts as a key signal that helps muscles respond to exercise. The researchers found that it plays an important role in reshaping muscle fibers, improving metabolism, and enhancing strength and endurance. It also helps protect muscles against damage and weakness associated with type 2 diabetes, raising the possibility of future treatments that preserve muscle function and make physical activity more manageable. Published in Nature Communications , the research was led by Professor Lee Roberts and funded by Diabetes UK and the Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council (BBRSC). Exercise prompts muscles to adapt so they can better handle future demands. Scientists are still investigating how the body coordinates these adaptations, and Roberts’ team wanted to understand whether those processes could inform treatments for chronic disease. L-BAIBA was already known for its effects on metabolism. In research published in 2014 , Roberts helped show that BAIBA could boost the fat-burning effects of exercise. L-BAIBA is now sold as a nutritional supplement, although the new findings concern its biological role and potential as a future treatment. The latest study extends that earlier work by identifying L-BAIBA as a regulator of muscle remodeling. Roberts, Professor of Molecular Physiology and Metabolism at the University of Leeds, said, “Our research identifies L-BAIBA as an exercise-induced signal that helps muscles adapt, improve their metabolic capacity and ability to contract, and ultimately enhances physical performance. “This gives us exciting new insight into how exercise benefits the body and highlights a promising target for future therapies aimed at preserving muscle function in chronic conditions such as diabetes.” L-BAIBA’s protective effects could be particularly valuable for people with type 2 diabetes, who can experience muscle loss, declining strength, and impaired metabolism. Weakness and fatigue can make exercise harder, creating a barrier to an activity that helps manage the condition. Future treatments targeting L-BAIBA could help people stay active by improving their muscles’ resistance to fatigue. The need for better ways to manage type 2 diabetes is growing as the condition becomes more common among younger adults. Cases among people under 40 are now increasing faster than those among people over 40. The condition can lead to serious complications, including heart attacks and strokes, and develops through a complex mix of factors, with risk influenced by age, ethnicity, genetics, and living with overweight or obesity. Anna Morris, Assistant Director of Research Strategy and Partnership at Diabetes UK, said: “Exercise plays an important role in managing type 2 diabetes, but for many people muscle weakness and fatigue can make staying active a real challenge. This research helps us better understand how muscles adapt to exercise and identifies a potential new target for improving muscle health. While these findings are still at an early stage, they could help shape future approaches that support people with type 2 diabetes to remain active and live healthier, longer lives.” Reference: “The metabokine β-aminoisobutyric acid mediates exercise performance and skeletal muscle adaptation through a PGC1α-BAIBA-PPARδ axis” by Helene N. Moriscot, Pim Knuiman, Koen Manusama, Marco Mensink, Irvin Teh, Jurgen E. Schneider, Richard Cubbon, Guy S. Taylor, Daniel J. West, David J. Beech, T. Scott Bowen and Lee D. Roberts, 18 August 2026, Nature Communications . DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-76307-8 Never miss a breakthrough: Join the SciTechDaily newsletter. Follow us on Google and Google News .

content: A supplement containing a substance naturally made by gut bacteria increased blood flow to a memory-related brain region in adults with obesity, raising new questions about its potential benefits. When the brain works harder, it needs more blood to supply oxygen and nutrients. For people with obesity, changes in blood vessel function can affect circulation, raising questions about how well the brain responds to these demands. A new clinical trial suggests a dietary supplement could help increase blood flow during mental activity, although researchers have yet to show that it improves memory. Researchers at the University of Oklahoma investigated urolithin A, a substance produced when certain gut bacteria break down compounds found in foods such as strawberries, pomegranates, and walnuts. The amount people naturally produce varies, and existing research suggests that production declines with age and increasing body mass index. Urolithin A is also available as a dietary supplement. In the randomized clinical trial, published in JAMA Network Open , 50 adults with obesity, ages 40 to 64, received either 1,000 milligrams of urolithin A daily or a placebo for four weeks. Participants taking the supplement showed a greater increase in blood flow to the brain while completing a challenging memory task. The difference was especially noticeable in the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, an area involved in holding and using information over short periods. However, researchers found no significant improvements in blood vessel function in the arm or performance on memory tests. “The brain needs an adequate supply of blood to meet the demands of mental activity,” said first author Ana Clara da Costa Pinaffi Langley, Ph.D., an assistant professor in the Department of Nutritional Sciences at the OU College of Allied Health on the OU Harold Hamm Health Campus. “We found that urolithin A increased blood flow to the brain during a memory task, suggesting the supplement may help the brain meet its increased need for oxygen and nutrients when it is working harder. We plan to conduct more research to understand what this finding means for brain health.” According to the researchers, this is the first human study to report an effect of urolithin A on blood vessel function in the brain. The supplement was well-tolerated, although the trial involved relatively few participants at a single research site. Longer studies with larger groups will be needed to determine whether the changes in blood flow lead to lasting health benefits. “These findings offer an interesting starting point for understanding how urolithin A affects the brain,” said study co-author Andriy Yabluchanskiy, M.D., Ph.D., an associate professor in the Department of Neurosurgery at the OU College of Medicine. “Although we saw increased blood flow to the brain during mental activity, participants did not demonstrate measurable improvements in memory or attention. Future studies will need to determine whether taking the supplement for a longer period leads to meaningful improvements in cognitive function or other health benefits.” The researchers ultimately hope to find ways to help people maintain their cognitive health as they age. “The idea is to mitigate cognitive decline,” Langley said. “We want to expand the time that people are living healthier lives.” Reference: “Urolithin A and Endothelial and Cerebrovascular Function in Middle-Aged Adults With Obesity: A Randomized Clinical Trial” by Ana Clara da Costa Pinaffi-Langley, Rafal Gulej, Zalan Kaposzta, Zsofia Szarvas, Ali Shahriari, Henry Kinnard, Bryan Ticer, Camila B. Pinto, Peter Mukli, Mihaly Muranyi, Cheryl Adams, Jeng Kong, Leah Anderson, Stefano Tarantini, Yan Daniel Zhao, Norman G. Hord and Andriy Yabluchanskiy, 9 October 2026, JAMA Network Open . DOI: 10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2026.38047 Research reported in this publication was supported by the American Heart Association (grant No. 24DIVSUP1282484 awarded to Dr da Costa Pinaffi-Langley) and the Reynolds Foundation. title: Why SNL’s ‘Sister’ sketch hit a nerve about the reality of caregiving
content: On “Saturday Night Live,” a pre-recorded segment called “ Sister ” hit too close to home for some, and others say the segment helped them finally feel seen. In the sketch, comedian John Mulaney pitches a care system for elderly parents that offers a live-in 24-hour caregiver who can be activated instantly with a simple text: “dad fell.” It’s called Sister. One message, and your actual sister will “quit her job, break her lease and move halfway across the country to take care of him,” all for free. “Years of internalized sexism warp Sister’s brain into thinking caretaking is her responsibility and somehow not yours,” a doctor, played by “SNL” cast member Mikey Day, explains. “Next, your text arrives, instantly activating her, and that’s it, you’re done for life. See you at the funeral.” Millions have watched the skit on YouTube, and it’s lighting up caregiver forums nationwide. As soon as the segment aired, Dr. Donna Benton, director of the USC Family Caregiver Support Center, was flooded with emails and texts. “It hit a nerve, obviously, with many, many women. And my whole reaction is ‘Yeah, I’ve been saying this for how long?’” Her research characterizing caregiving in California over the past several decades shows a 70-30 split, with women handling most of the caregiving. “That hasn’t changed in 40 years,” Benton said. But the good thing about the “SNL” sketch, she said, is that it prompted people who saw it to reach out “saying, ‘What can we do? How can we address this?’” “If this starts a new national conversation, that will be a success.” There’s a good chance you will end up caring for an aging parent at some point, especially if you’re a woman. Most older people with long-term care needs in the United States rely exclusively on family and friends to help them. “We think the way our parents were in their 50s and 60s will continue forever. But when you cross that 80-year-old mark, most older adults are going to need help,” Benton said. Nearly 1 in 5 adults — 51 million Americans — are caregivers for loved ones 50 and older. Three in 5 family caregivers are women, according to AARP research. “The female caregiver, the sister, the daughter, the cousin, the neighbor are stepping in to fill the gaps in what is a national care crisis,” said Jason Resendez, president and CEO of the National Alliance for Caregiving, a research and policy group. This phenomenon is so common that it has even earned a nickname: “the daughter tax.” Caregiving often begins with what experts call “caregiver creep.” Adult children run errands for their parents at first, but as their parent becomes frailer, the children step in to take on more. Even if there are multiple children in the family, it’s typically a sister, not a brother, who shoulders the bulk of the caregiving. An influential 2017 study quantified the time daughters versus sons spend on care and found that daughters spend more than twice as much time caring for their aging parents as sons do. On average, daughters logged 12.3 hours of care each month, compared with just 5.6 hours for sons. “It’s hardly surprising to say that women provide more care,” said study co-author Dr. Angelina Grigoryeva, an assistant professor in the sociology department at the University of Toronto. It’s mostly women who oversee a parent’s medication, drive them to the doctor, prepare meals, clean homes, battle insurance companies and do everything they can to keep their parents physically safe. And, studies show , most do it without formal or financial support, often at such a great cost to themselves physically, emotionally and financially that researchers call caregivers “invisible second patients.” “Caregiving is not an easy task. It is one thing to give a baby a bath, imagine having to give a bath to an adult person,” Grigoryeva said. “It’s also more stressful. And many American women have to provide childcare and elder care at the same time, and it all comes at a cost.” While societal expectations are that women are the more nurturing gender, much of elderly parent caregiving is learned on the fly with no real time for trial and error. “It can start with a call from your mom that she fell, so it’s hard to prepare for this until you’re really in the thick of it,” said Debra Whitman, chief public policy officer at AARP. And the caregiving role can last decades. Often, the physical impact of caregiving hits women harder than men. Nearly 40% of women who are caregivers say that caregiving has taken a negative toll on their physical health, compared with 26% of men. It also strains women’s mental health, with 47% of women saying caring for an aging parent has weighed on their emotional well-being. There is no federal paid family leave and no job protection for people who step away to care for an aging parent. Although 44% of people who are caregivers work full-time, sometimes an aging parent’s needs become so great that caregivers leave the workforce, move to part-time work or retire early. “If you have to take time off of work, you also lose your health benefits, you lose access to retirement savings or pensions, and you later take a hit on your Social Security,” said Whitman. She noted that altogether, an average working caregiver forfeits about $120,500 in wages, retirement savings and Social Security. If a caregiver can work, they will often settle for a more flexible position that pays less or comes with a less desirable shift. Even when they return to work after an elderly parent dies, caregivers are much more likely to earn lower wages, land a “benefit-poor” job and receive reduced retirement benefits, research shows. The person who provides care for their parent also bears the most out-of-pocket expenses , and those expenses have climbed sharply. AARP estimates that family caregivers spend an average of $11,508 a year out of pocket, almost 60% more than they did in 2021. Caregivers of a parent with Alzheimer’s or another form of dementia shell out even more, with an average of $15,846 a year. In total, family caregivers devote 31% of their household income to caregiving expenses, according to an October AARP research report. AARP has been urging Congress to offer tax credits for these out-of-pocket expenses. Benton also points to the added emotional labor highlighted in the SNL sketch. Mulaney explains that Sister will talk to doctors on the phone, talk to insurance companies on the phone and talk to pharmacists on the phone. “Speak to human. Speak to human,” the sister says into her speakerphone. Benton said that exchange shows the caregiving problem is not just about unequal gender roles; it also underscores how much systems-level change is needed. “Systems have pushed us where we can’t even talk to a person. You have to make three phone calls and navigate this very complex healthcare system, and it’s very frustrating,” Benton said. Benton said social service systems are dramatically underfunded. And many don’t realize that Medicare does not pay for long-term or nursing home care that would help with daily activities like bathing, dressing or eating. “We don’t have a good national long-term strategy for caregiving and that puts more pressures back on the families and on women in particular,” Benton said. “Systems aren’t helping us as caregivers. It’s actually making it harder.” What can help as parents age, AARP’s Whitman said, is to have an open conversation before the need arises about what should happen if a parent requires help. “Communication is really important, and so is dividing up responsibilities,” she said. It’s also important to make room for the caregiver to ask for help. A shared calendar to manage tasks can help, and it’s important to frame caregiving as a team activity. It’s easier to get people to step up when using words “we” and “together” instead of saying “you.” It’s also important to ask for help before a caregiver feels overwhelmed. Reaching out is not a sign of weakness. Ultimately, though, Benton believes a broader conversation is needed about systems outside the home, and the belief that women have to do it all. “I tend to think that the systems have to change because these systems impact women in a different way that it does men,” Benton said. That sense that women think they are the ones who have to take on the caregiver role – even if it hurts them personally – doesn’t happen organically. “Part of the internalized expectations comes from the fact that we don’t have external options,” she said. Benton asks why caregiving can’t generate a certain amount of credits for Social Security, or why there aren’t tax breaks for people who have to take time off to provide elder or child care. “With our aging population, we are going to have more older adults than younger children,” she said. “So elder care is going to be even more of the norm in the next 10 years, and this system we have now is not sustainable long-term.”

final_quality.reason: The article reports a substantive and important development in the category of health, specifically the reality of caregiving, and provides a clear reason for readers to care, highlighting the significance of the issue and the potential for a national conversation.
